_notes: CHAPTER 1, COMPLETE (opening arc: owner brief 2026-08-04; back half:
2026-08-08, from chapters/01-case-file-wax-and-wick.md as amended).
The opening arc, in the order the board offers it:
follow_the_thread -- the obvious move, tried first: the thread is CUT
(owner 2026-08-10: 'why does he not just follow
that thread' -- now he does, and the player
chooses which of the two starting jobs to take)
find_the_magpie   -- the Exchange, and gleam being worth something
the_carrying      -- the witches come for her; the Case Board opens
what_i_saw        -- Ash goes back over last night alone (Crossing)
ask_the_rats      -- the Ratsmeet, and how to ask a question (Testimony)
sharpen_the_claws -- growth: he decides to get harder to kill
the_wake          -- her funeral; her last seam, sewn by the player
Then the investigation proper, chained on evidence, not on quest ids:
creditors            -- the counting-house heist; the ledger; BODKIN ENTERS
the_lamplighters_talk-- Merrow's round, her testimony, the hall ward mended
the_ward_that_failed -- the Wickhouse; the backward seam; Remembered Day 1
an_audience_of_wax   -- the Tallowman, Wick's books, the verdict choice
Sides: night_rounds / garden_route / empty_coat (fight-chains with faces),
the_milk_debt (Tansy + the Gentleman's paper), the_pigeon_ballot (the
murder-night seed; needs the docket, so its break is always possible).
Quests are ProwlScript `steps`: fight, story, flashback, minigame, lesson.
Lessons play ONCE (data/lessons.json) and replay from the Casebook. A
story step may gate on `when_minigame` success/loss -- a lost testimony
must never be followed by the page narrating the confession (law 17).
GATING: the_carrying is the only CORE work after the Magpie, because a
body being carried out of your house does not wait its turn. The three
middle jobs open together; the_wake waits for all three; the back half
waits for the_wake and then chains itself on the evidence each lead
yields. Every Bodkin line is LITERALLY TRUE (docs/design/the-unraveler.md
-- read it before giving him a single new word).

follow_the_thread.name: The Thread Itself
follow_the_thread.board_card: One strand of her thread still runs out under the window and into the city. The obvious thing is to follow it. I am going to do the obvious thing.

lines: The strand under the window, still running, still hers. Every other thread in this house was cut clean — nobody cut THIS one.

Magic is needlework. Her words, said at the table like a recipe: witches stitch the world, and cats are among the few things that can see the seam. The WEFT, she called it — every thread of everything, crossing.
Follow it, then. Paw on the line, like tracking a fly across a window.
The strand under the window again, patient the way only thread is. It did not go anywhere. I did.
Paw on the line. From the top.
It runs the rooftops the way I do — the clean route, chimney to chimney, never crossing an open street. Whoever it belongs to knows this city the way the city hopes nobody does.
And where it crosses the gutter-line, something has found it first: a wisp, drinking the hum off it the way moths drink a lamp.
It is on HER thread. That is not trespass. That is grave-robbing.
Past the lane the thread drops to street level and runs straight for the Mere — and the fog stands up to meet it, thick as a held breath.
There is no fighting through this. There is only getting across it without losing the line.

on_loss_lines: I come out three streets wrong, with the line lost twice and found twice.
The fog wanted the thread walked away from. Noted, and declined.

lines: At the Mere-edge the thread runs out over the sea-wall and stops. Mid-air. Above the water.
Not frayed. Not worn through. CUT — one clean bite, the same as the threads on her walls, by something that could SEE it. Almost nothing can see them.
Whoever ended this trail knew exactly what a cat would try first, and closed that door in my face.
So the thread is not a road. It is an answer of its own: the one who did this reads the Weft, cuts clean, and did not want to be followed home across the water.
A trail closed on purpose has to be bought open, and the Shambles keeps a fence who knows everyone worth asking.
The long way round, then. Nobody said the obvious thing would be the quick one.

find_the_magpie.name: Find the Magpie
find_the_magpie.board_card: A cat with a question and no answers needs a fence. Brindle keeps a stall in the Shambles and keeps everything else besides.

steps.art_desc: The Shambles after hours: stalls shuttered under canvas, one lit fence's stall at the lane's end with a magpie behind it, Ash in his red kerchief walking toward it with a thimble in his mouth
lines: I cannot stay in this room tonight, and the room knows it. The thread runs into the city, and the city sells answers.
Brindle keeps a stall in the Shambles after the market has gone to bed, and nobody talks for nothing. That is the first true thing about Hollowmere.
So I bring payment: her second-best thimble, carried in my own mouth, because a cat has no pockets. Dignity and I will discuss it later.
Down the Shambles again, the thimble back in my teeth. It kept. Dignity did not.
Unfinished work waits. That is the whole of its nature.
Halfway down the Shambles, something comes up out of a drain for the shine in my mouth.
A gutter-wisp — and it is not after ME at all. It wants the thimble: witch's silver, small enough to steal.
Small lies and small valuables. It cannot tell the difference and it has never once needed to.
The drain is loud again — the shine in my mouth rings them up like a bell.
Rooms this cheap never stay empty.

steps.art_desc: Brindle the magpie fence behind a market stall of buttons, teeth and small keys, one bright eye, night market lanterns
lines: I arrive at the stall with the thimble still in my teeth and my dignity somewhere behind me on the cobbles.

Brindle is on her perch above the shutters, black and white with that oil-slick green in the wing, doing the thing magpies do that looks like idleness and is inventory. She watches me the length of the lane and speaks before I have set the thimble down.
'You are the witch's cat.' — 'Was,' I say. She does not say sorry, and I like her enormously for it. Sorry is what people say instead of anything useful.
'Back,' says Brindle, before I have said anything at all. Fences know their street; knowing it is the whole trade.
Being remembered in this city is halfway to a friendship — and all the way to a debt.
'Clear the wisps out of my back alley and we can have a conversation like professionals.'
She has not touched the thimble. 'Three nights they have been in my stock, hunting anything with a seal or a shine on it, and I am one bird.'
A fence with a wisp problem. Payment, it turns out, comes in kinds.
'The alley, pet. Three nights of wisps in my stock, and I am one bird. Clear it, then the conversation.' She has not touched the thimble.
'I need to know who was on Needle Lane last night.'
'Right,' says Brindle, when the alley is quiet. 'You're not useless. That's the whole interview.' She takes the thimble at last, and holds it a moment longer than trade requires.
'Bring me buttons and I'll remember harder. Doors open now. Mind the step.'

the_carrying.name: The Carrying
the_carrying.board_card: There are women at the door of the house. They have brought a sheet. This is not something to be attended — it is something to be witnessed.

lines: Three witches came at first light. Nobody sent for them. I asked, later, how they knew.
'Nine seats,' Cardew said. 'One rope between the nine of us. A seat goes out, the weight comes onto the rest, and you feel it in your wrists whether you're minding or not.'
She had felt it at dusk, in her own kitchen, with a pan in her hand. I asked why she waited for morning. 'You don't walk Needle Lane in the dark. Not while something is still —'
They do not knock. Witches do not knock at a house where a witch has died; a knock asks a question, and the house has already answered it.
Mother Cardew is the eldest of the Circuit, and it was eight seats now, though nobody had said so aloud yet in that room.

She is small and grey and folded, like something kept a long time in a drawer. Her eyes went around the parlor once, at working speed, and I watched her see everything. The cut threads. The cold kettle off the fire, which nobody could account for and nobody asked about. Elspeth.
Behind her, two young ones I did not know: one carrying folded linen, undyed, and one carrying nothing but her own held breath.
I was on the arm of the chair. I had been on the arm of the chair all night. I did not get down.

steps.art_desc: Three witches in grey lifting a shrouded body from a chair in a cold parlor at dawn, a black cat watching from the mantel
lines: They lifted her the way you lift someone who might wake. That is the thing I will allow them, all three, forever.
The young one who had been carrying her own breath let it go in the doorway, once, in a small ragged sound she will be embarrassed about for years. It was the correct sound.
Cardew stopped at the door and looked back at the walls. Forty years of workings hanging cut and dead at one tidy height.

'Who did this to the room,' she says. Not a question. Burglars take things, and nothing here was taken: not the thimbles, not the bolt of moon-colored cloth worth a bargeman's year, not the rings on the hand of the woman in the chair.
And then Cardew was looking at me. Everyone else was looking at the floor — that is what people do around a dead witch's cat.
She looked straight at me, colleague to colleague, and waited.
One chance to be taken seriously. A cat who yowls is comforted. A cat who performs is petted.
choices: Tell her exactly what came in the door.
Say nothing. Watch what she does with silence.
Ask what unpicks a witch's own stitching.
steps.art_desc: The workroom doorway from inside: cut threads hanging the length of the frame, scissors and pinned patterns on the table, cold morning light

lines: I told it, all of it, in order, as she taught me anything worth saying should go: the lamps, the pigeons, the emptied hall, her thread on the lamp-hook, the fog with sleeves. The shape in the doorway that decided I was not an interruption.
Cats can speak to those who trouble to listen, and most people do not trouble. Cardew listened the whole way through without moving.
Then she said, quieter, to nobody: 'Again.'
She put the word down like something she had not meant to be holding. I filed it. AGAIN means BEFORE, and a thing that has done this before has habits, and habits can be found.
I say nothing. Cats are good at nothing; it is most of what we do.
She waits me out, which nobody does, and then gives up first, which nobody does either.
'Suit yourself.' At the door she stops. 'It has happened before. Twice that I will admit to.' A pause. 'Mind the room, cat. Rooms hold a while. After that —'
She did not finish it. I think the end of that sentence had worn off her a long time ago and she had stopped missing it.
'What unpicks a witch's own stitching?' I ask.
The room gets colder in a way the room is not responsible for.
'Something that learned it from her,' says Cardew. 'Or from one of us.' She looks at her two frightened girls, and does not look at them for quite long enough.
The day-side came at nine. Two constables, not unkind. The younger one wiped his boots on the mat, which I record in his favour.

They tried the window catch. They looked at the hearth. All around them hung forty years of workings cut through at one tidy height, and they stood in the middle of it and saw an old woman dead in her chair behind a door locked from the inside.
'Heart, most like,' the older one said. 'At her age.' The younger one wrote that down, stepped twice over a thing under the window I had not yet found, and they were gone in ten minutes.

Nor is there anybody on the night-side whose office this is. The Circuit mends. The Court of Whiskers serves papers. The Hollow Court files the dead and says so. The Magpie sells what it knows to whoever is buying.
None of them owns a killing. I did that arithmetic twice, because I did not care for the answer.
So I minded the room. I went over it the way she went over a hem: slowly, twice, against the nap.
Under everything, faint, something that did not belong: pond-bottom. Old rope. Patient water. The Mere has a smell, and the Mere does not come up to Thimblefield, and it had been in this room.

And under the window, where the curtain hem brushes the boards, the thing the constable stepped over twice. A candle stub. Beeswax, burned an inch down and pinched out, stamped near the base with the bee.
She burned tallow her whole life. Good witch-made tallow, smoky and stubborn like her. She called beeswax the rich man's smell and would not have it in the house.
Somebody else's light had been in this parlor.
And out of that inch of wax I built the man who left it. What follows is a thing I built, not a thing I found, and I am setting it down the way I had it.

An inch of beeswax is about an hour. Somebody sat in this parlor an hour before she died, with a light of his own, brought in his own pocket. He did not mean to sit in the dark and he did not mean to use hers. Then he pinched the wick out with his fingers and did not trouble to take the stub away.
An hour of lit window on Needle Lane, with forty neighbours who have nothing better to do than notice. It should have been seen.
Then I remembered the shutters, closed for the first time in fifteen years, and thought: of course. He closed them. He shut the lane out, lit his own candle, and settled down to wait for her.
I was pleased with that.

what_i_saw.name: What I Saw
what_i_saw.board_card: Nobody asked me to do this. I am going to walk last night again, in order, until the order of it gives something up.

lines: A thing I have learned about being the only witness: everyone believes you, and nobody acts on it.
So. From the top: the roof, the market, the lane, the lamps. Not for anybody — for the order of it.
The gutter first, where the wisp came up for my little lie. There is another one in it tonight. There is always another one.
The lamps on Needle Lane are still out. Nobody has been up the ladders — the Lamplighters are not coming, which is itself a fact.
And the fog off the Mere has come up over the whole street, sitting where fog does not sit, thick as a held breath.
There is no fighting through this. There is only getting across it.

on_loss_lines: I come out of it four streets wrong and shaking, which is data of a kind.
Whatever is in that fog does not want the lane walked. Noted.

lines: Out the far end, at the mouth of the lane, in the gutter where a wheel would throw it:
A cart docket. Chandlers' paper — the bee in the corner — for a delivery, night of, Needle Lane. And the consignee line filled in by a hand that then thought better of it and scratched it out.
Somebody drove a cart down a street with no lamps on it, at night, and did not want to be the sort of person who had. That takes a professional. That takes a QUIET one.
The long way round, then — streets I know, to the lane's far mouth, arriving like a tourist.
And there, in the gutter where a wheel would throw it: a cart docket. Chandlers' paper — the bee in the corner — night of, Needle Lane, consignee scratched out.
Somebody drove a cart down a dark street and did not want to have. That takes a professional. That takes a QUIET one.

ask_the_rats.name: Ask the Rats
ask_the_rats.board_card: Nothing crosses this city at night without a rat watching it and pricing the information. Brindle says go to the Ratsmeet. Brindle says wear my patience.

lines: The Ratsmeet convenes under the fish market in the hour the ice melts, and every rat in Hollowmere sends somebody.
There is a protocol. You do not eat anybody. You do not say 'trap' or 'terrier'. You do not be a cat about it. (Once. We do not discuss the terrier.)
And you do not argue with the doorman. The doorman is a goose. Rats are not stupid: a goose cannot be bribed, and has never once liked a cat.

steps.art_desc: The boss of the Ratsmeet: an ancient grey rat on a throne of market crates under a fish market, chalk tallies and ledgers around him
lines: Their boss is grey to the point of transparency. He will tell you he remembers the ninth bell. Nobody argues with him.
'The witch's cat,' he says. 'We had a lively night. Everyone had a lively night.'
He will talk. Rats always talk — for a price, in a shape. While he finishes his ice, I limber up on the doorman.

on_loss_lines: He tells it beautifully and I cannot get a claw into any of it.
'Come back when you know more,' he says, which is the politest possible way to bill me for an hour of rat time.

lines: A cart with no chandler on it, and a gentleman behind it going nowhere in particular. The Grey Boss charges honest rates once he has stopped lying.
You cannot clear out of an empty street. I will be keeping that one.
By morning the Chandlers will know a cat was asking about their cart. Good.
A rat's silence is a price list. He knows the lane's story; the lane knows; I am the only one paying retail.
Still: 'a lively night,' he called it, on a lane he swears was empty. Empty lanes are not lively. I will come back armed.
By morning the Chandlers will know a cat was asking about Needle Lane. Word is the one thing this market gives away free.

sharpen_the_claws.name: Sharpen the Claws
sharpen_the_claws.board_card: The thing in the parlor went through me like I was a curtain. That is not happening a second time. There is a wall behind the tannery that nobody minds about.

lines: Here is the part nobody puts in the stories: I lost.
It came into her house and I did everything I know how to do, and it did not even hurry.
I am fifteen. I had put my working nights away without telling anybody, there being nobody to tell. Whatever I was at eight is not in this body, and I am not going to be given it back.
So I will go and get some of it again, deliberately, too late, and badly. That is still faster than waiting to be improved by events.
First: the Watch goose behind the tannery, which has never lost an argument in its life. That is what makes it worth arguing with.
Elspeth used to say the difference between brave and stupid is about four seconds of looking. Watch it. THEN decide.
Next lesson: the dog at Number Twelve, who has eleven feet of chain, no appointments, and a standing offer to discuss territory.
Slower this time. Watch what the thing in front of you is going to do BEFORE deciding what you are going to do about it.
And one more thing, which is not fighting and is the reason for the fighting.
Her ward is still on the door frame, and it has a hole in it the size of the thing that walked through it.
She patched this door every autumn of my life while complaining about the weather. I have watched it four hundred times. Watching is not the same as doing. I am about to find that out.

on_win_lines: It holds. It is not her work — hers was invisible and mine can be seen from the street — but it holds.
Nothing comes through that door tonight that I have not agreed to.
on_loss_lines: I get most of it and the last corner will not take, and I sit with my nose an inch from the gap until it is light.
Fine. Not tonight, then. Tonight I just watch the door myself.

lines: There is a wall behind the tannery that has been holding up nothing at all for sixty years.

I go at it until my legs are wrong, and then a bit past that, and then I lie down in the dark and listen to my own heart being annoyed with me. In the morning my shoulder will not have come back. Some of it never will.
Better. Not enough. But the kind of not-enough that has a direction in it.

the_wake.name: The Wake
the_wake.board_card: They give a witch to the tide at the turn of the evening. That is the custom. Every guild will send somebody to be seen not caring, and I am expected to be decorative. She expected better.

steps.art_desc: A witch's funeral at the tideline at dusk: a shrouded figure on a low bier, women in grey, guild delegates at a careful distance, a black cat on a mooring post
lines: No one day-side troubles to know the rite, so I will tell it. No grave, no fire. A witch's work is thread, and thread must be tied off, not buried.
They sew the shroud shut over her in her own stitch, worked by whoever loved or owed her most, and give her to the water at slack tide.

The quay was fuller than I expected and emptier than she deserved. The Lamplighters sent four, everyone the hall has left, with their ladders shouldered and their lamps at half-wick, which is their mourning.

The Magpie Exchange sent a bird I did not yet know, watchful on a bollard, with one respectful button laid on the stones. And the Chandlers sent one man, early, in very good black, standing precisely where he could be seen being sorry.
Mother Cardew took the bone needle and the grey thread and began the shroud's last seam in Elspeth's own pattern. Four stitches in, she stopped.
She stood there with the linen raised in her unsteady hands, an old woman in front of a city, and I watched her courage fail in a way I would not wish on an enemy.
'I don't know her hand,' she said. Quietly. To the linen. 'Sixty years, and I don't know her hand.'
Nobody moved. The tide turned underneath us — you feel it through stone, through the pads of your feet, the moment the sea changes its mind — and the seam stood open four stitches.

I have watched those hands from a windowsill every evening of my life. Through fog, through frost-flowers, through my own reflection: the needle down, the thread drawn, the little tug at the end of each stitch like a word ending.
I know the hand better than I know my own name, which she also gave me, so it comes to the same thing.
I got up onto the bier. Somebody started forward to stop me, some notion of decency, and Cardew said 'Let him,' in a voice that ended the subject for a generation.

on_loss_lines: A cat is not built for needlework. I pushed the bone needle with a paw and drew the thread in my teeth, and the first stitch took me three tries, like the kettle.

The last corner beat me. Cardew finished it without a word about it. She does not say I did well; she puts one small hard hand flat on my back for a moment, which is not a thing witches do to cats they have just met.

lines: The seam closed. The tide took her without discussion — no speeches, no splash, the grey linen going down through the grey water until it was a paleness, and then a memory.
One lamplighter forgot not to salute.

Then Cardew did the thing for which I will forgive her everything else, always. In front of the guild delegates and the roofline and the man in very good black, she bent down. It cost her; I heard her knees pay it.
She tied a small grey knot into the thread at my chest, where the whole Weft could read it. 'A debt,' she said. 'Mine. You'll know.'
Then, walking me back up the quay while the crowd made itself busy elsewhere, low, for my ears alone:

'It has happened twice before. Both times a stitcher. The Tatterstage's lead player, forty years gone — one of ours, though the playbills never knew it. And Widow Sarn of Hemlock Row, three winters after. She sewed sails. She taught half the quay to mend nets. Her terrier sat out two winters on her step, waiting to be let in.'
'Nobody looked, either time. The Circuit closed the files. I signed the closing.' She did not finish that thought out loud. 'I'm too old to open them again. Too watched, as well.'
I asked who would look now.

'Seven of us,' she said, 'holding what she held. Ten years of her work, and there's a thing under this town that wants a hand on it every hour of the night.' She turned her own hand over and looked at it. 'There's no spare hand in this city to go asking who. So nobody will look.'

She stopped at the sea-wall and looked at the water a while. 'You are neither.' A pause. 'You were her ninth, you know. She'd never say what she meant by the count.' Another. 'Find who did this, cat. I'll hold what doors I have left.'
Ninth. I filed the word next to AGAIN, in the drawer of things said to me that were heavier than the sayer knew.
Home, then, to a house with nobody in it. The lamps went up along her street. Most of them. Two dark.

The kettle sat where I left it, off the fire, on the cold hearthstone, and of everything in that room it was the wrongest thing — because a kettle off the fire is a kettle finished, and nothing here is finished. Nothing here has even begun.
My whole job used to be: be somewhere warm at the correct time.
All right, then. New job.

creditors.name: Creditors
creditors.board_card: The counting-house keeps paper on everything the Chandlers do. Somebody should read it. Cats cannot be arrested, only despised.

lines: Brindle first. I bring her the docket, because paper is her native language and mine only by adoption.

She reads it head cocked, one eye at a time: the watermark, the fold-grease, the ink that had been wet in fog. 'Counting-house paper. Chandlers'. This is the flimsy, the copy that rides with the cart.'

Then she flicks the scrap flat with one black claw to take the corner, and stops. Half a second, no longer. Her working eye sits on the cart-slot seal and does not travel, and her cocked head comes level while it sits there.
Then she goes on as though the seal were weather. If I had been less new to all this I would have asked her what she had just decided not to say. I was new. I filed it instead.
'The originals live under the ledgers, second yard off Wick Row. Mind the night shift, pet.'
Wickrow after dark is the best-lit district in the city. Every doorway wears a little flame: a lamp over the door, a burning stub in the window above it, candle-boxes along the sills.
Every flame is a warded bee, burning in its own wax and billed to the tenants by the quarter. Other streets buy locks. Wickrow buys light. That is stock control.

I go in over the roofs and drop to the yards where the roofs run out, and meet the night shift. The night shift is a hound: not the honest kind that discusses territory from the end of a chain, but a counting-house hound, off its chain, walked yard to yard and turned loose in each one.

The yard is a box and the box is his. Wall on three sides, tarred smooth, nothing in it a claw could use. The gate stands open at his back, which is the whole art of a yard dog — he does not have to catch you, he only has to go on standing between you and the one hole.
Whatever settled that yard, it was not speed. I have none to bring to a hound and have not had for years. What a dog built like that cannot do is change his mind inside his own length.
So I made him commit and went under his head on the side he had to swing his whole body to answer. I record it that way because that is how it went.

But it cost me the quiet. Somewhere across the yards the keys stopped counting, and the lantern came around, and boots — more than one pair — and I came off the wall low and fast into an alley-mouth that was blind.
A paw hooked my scruff and hauled me sideways through a gap I had not seen, and held me in a doorway's dead shadow while the watch went past close enough to smell the supper on them.

A grey tom, considering me from the dark. Old, big-boned under a coat that has seen weather. One eye, half of one ear, and the stillness of a creature that has spent a long time being exactly as visible as it chooses.
'You fight like a housecat,' he says. — 'I was one.' — 'Were,' he agrees, and does not say sorry, which makes two of them now I like for it.
He was the first creature since the parlor to put a paw on me, and the paw was sure, and something in me that had been walking on three legs since the kettle went quiet put its fourth foot down.
'Watch the paws, not the claws,' he says. 'Claws are a rumor. Paws are an appointment. The dog told you where he would be four moves before he got there, and you were reading the teeth.'
'Wax door, far side, under the loading beam. The counting room is behind it, and Wick's paper is worth the reading.'
'You know what I am looking for,' I said. It was not a question and he did not treat it as one. 'I knew your witch to look at,' he says. 'Everyone did.'
Then he gave me one more thing I had not asked for, flat, and worn smooth with saying.

'You will be under other people's roofs all season, so have this one. Nobody collects off a lit candle. You take a house's light, you take its salt, you take its fire: take any of the three and you take nothing else under that roof that night. Not a debt. Not a favor. Not a mouse.'

The one eye came around at me. 'It is not manners. Manners you can decline. It is older than the Hollow Court and older than the desk they keep in it, and it was old before anybody thought of writing things down.'
'Bodkin,' he says at the gap in the fence, his name, given as the old ones give it, once, take it or leave it. Gone over with no more noise than a thought. The name meant nothing to me then.

on_loss_lines: The ward re-crosses itself faster than I can read it, and somewhere below a bell taps twice, politely.
The counting-house knows a cat is in it. Fine. Cats have been despised by better buildings than this one.

lines: Under the ledgers, exactly where the flimsy's watermark said they would be, the originals. And in the originals, her name.

VANE, in a strong small impatient hand. Instruction after instruction, dated inside one single week of this spring. The tallow debt to the renderers' yard. Two winters' rent on the workroom before the good years. The chandlery account, seven years old, forgiven-in-name and never in law.
'Buy it quiet, pay the premium for quiet, and call it due Lady's Day.' Every debt my witch owed in the world, bought up in seven days, by one buyer.
I made myself read it twice, because the first reading had a red wash over it and red is not a reading light.

A man who buys every debt you owe and calls them due on one date is not planning your murder. He is planning your EVICTION. You do not go to the expense of killing a woman you have spent a premium to lawfully destroy.
And you particularly do not kill her if her needlework holds shut something you profit by. A dead seamstress mends nothing. So whose light was burning in her parlor?
Over the yards and out, with a page of a rich man's handwriting folded into my shadow.
Paper says what Wick WANTED. Paper does not say what he DID. For that you need people who watch the Chandlers professionally, and hate them fluently.
The Lamplighters' hall keeps a light burning at the door these days. Time it answered some questions.

the_lamplighters_talk.name: The Lamplighters Talk
the_lamplighters_talk.board_card: The Lamplighters hate the Chandlers professionally. Hate is chatty — and their hall has questions of its own about that night.

steps.art_desc: The Lamplighters' hall by night: empty coats on pegs over boots nobody came back for, a chalk tally board, four lamplighters at one lamp, Ash in his red kerchief at the door
lines: The Lamplighters' hall burns lamps at its own door. That costs a guild that cannot spare the oil: their own light, spent outward at the dark, all night, every night, as a point of order.
I stopped on the wall opposite and read the front of that building like a notice. We are not gone. We light what we have. Come home.

Inside, one cold room. Most of the coats on the pegs hang over boots nobody has come back for — pairs of boots, toes out, waiting, under coats that keep their shapes the way the wraith on Needle Lane kept a shape.
Forty lamplighters used to walk Hollowmere. What is left of the guild fits in that room, around one lamp, with room to spare. It goes quiet when a cat comes in.
They knew me the moment I came in. THE WITCH'S CAT went around the room the way words go around a room full of people not saying them, and the room braced.

The one to convince is obvious. Torn ear. Chalk on her paws — hands; I keep the ledger in my own tongue. A shift-boss's way of standing, facing the door, near the lamp, where the next bad news would have to go through her first.
Merrow.
choices: Lay the ledger page on the floor between us.
Ask after their missing, and listen.
Sit. Wait to be spoken to. Cats are good at nothing.

lines: The page goes down on the boards. Paper first is an auditor's manners, and the room reads it as such.
Merrow reads Wick's hand upside down, which tells me she has read it before. Other pages. Other nights.
'Paper,' she says. 'The Chandlers are made of it. Walk my round with me, cat. Rounds first. Paper after.'
I do the thing I have been carrying since the doorway, which has the advantage of being true: I look at the coats over the boots, and I ask after their missing.
The room stops bracing.

'Not dead,' says Merrow. Flat, fast, a door long since slammed on that word. 'The Court said not dead. Our filings came back MARKED: no appointments under those names. Eleven names. I file them again every week and they come back marked.'

'The day-side says contract work up the coast. Good money, no notice given. There is no paper in the world that says where a man is not.' She looks at the pegs. 'Their rounds are still walked. I walk two of them myself. Rounds first. Come.'
I sit. I am prepared to be furniture for an hour; furniture usually wins.
It takes four minutes. I am the first party to come into that hall and not open with the murder, and it settles something.
'Fine,' says Merrow, taking up her pole. 'You do manners. Walk my round with me and we will see what else you do.'
Her round is forty-one lamps, and something is walking it ahead of us. We both see it by the fifth: lamps lit at the round's head, dark again behind us.

Not blown. Not failed. DRUNK — wicks wet and whole, the little warded bees drained to grease. And the order of the darkening is the sequence her guild has walked so long it has worn a groove in the evening.
At the fifteenth we double back quiet and catch them at it. A pair of wisps, fat as lamp-oil themselves, working her lamps in sequence, one keeping watch while the other drinks.
Wisps do not do that. A wisp is appetite in a bottle. Appetite does not read route-maps, and it does not skip a bright lamp to keep a schedule.
Merrow plants the pole. 'Get them off my round, cat, and I will believe every next thing you say.'
One of them opens the flank the hound left me, which bleeds quietly for the rest of the night, and I say nothing about it and finish the round. She relights her lamps in her order to the round's end.
At the hall door she chalks a fresh tally on the wood, one stroke among hundreds, and I understand that the strokes are rounds completed since the night of the missing.
'You came about the night,' she says. 'Ask, then. I answer what is asked. No more.'
That is a doorway exactly the width of your own wits.

on_loss_lines: Merrow answers exactly what I ask, and I ask it wrong, and the wall of her holds.
'Out of questions?' She is not gloating. She is disappointed, which is worse.

lines: I did not ask who killed her, nor what happened to her missing. I asked what work Elspeth Vane did in Wickrow that nobody paid for.

Merrow looked at me the way you look at a colleague who has just found the fault you had walked past. Then she took down the shift-book, opened it to a page her thumb knew, and laid it where I could read.
'That is Wick's hand,' she says, tapping the requisition. 'And that is the night nobody signed.'

Two facing pages: for two years, at the turn of every season and after every hard blow off the Mere, ward-shifts at the Wickhouse, logged, walked, witnessed, and paid to nobody. The escort-lamplighter's fee stood in the book every time. The stitcher's fee stood blank every time.
Nobody sews free. She least of anyone — I have watched her price a churn-blessing to the ha'penny and then chase the ha'penny.

Questions are not the only tool in a hall full of torn things. Merrow hands me the tally anyway — two years of Wickhouse ward-shifts, paid to nobody — because the tally is her own grievance, and grievances want witnesses.
Nobody sews free. Elspeth least of all. Whatever is in the Wickhouse, she thought it was worth her thread.
Behind the meeting-board their own ward hangs torn: the hall's hem, ripped the night of the missing and left that way, because the one who always mended it is one of the coats.
They have been living inside a torn ward every night since, sooner than let anyone else touch her seam.
Merrow sees me looking. The whole room sees Merrow seeing. Cats inspect seams, by ancient arrangement.
Getting up on the meeting-board takes me two tries with that flank, and the whole room watches me take them.

on_win_lines: I mend their ward in front of everybody, better than I did the parlor door, because the parlor door taught me how.
When it is done the hall hums faintly, low, under the talk. One of the four remaining lamplighters puts his face in his hands. Everyone else looks at the lamp.
on_loss_lines: I patch what will take, and the last gap beats me, and Merrow puts her own hand over it without a word.
'First mend this hall has had since the night,' she says. 'Somebody had to be first.'

lines: Merrow walks me to the door. At the threshold, in front of her whole guild, she ties a lamplighter's knot into the thread at my chest — rough work, honest, tight — where the entire Weft can read it.
'The hall owes the cat,' she says, for the room.
And then, bending close, for me alone, in the voice she keeps for the end of bad shifts: 'Wisps do not learn a route. Somebody taught them the taste. Find the teacher.'
The Wickhouse next. Her last work is holding a rich man's dark shut, and I want to know what it is holding it shut ON.

the_ward_that_failed.name: The Ward That Failed
the_ward_that_failed.board_card: The Wickhouse ward is Elspeth's stitching, kept for free on a warehouse full of dark. Go read her last work. Bring nothing that burns.

lines: The Wickhouse squats on the Mere-edge, fat as a tick, warded to the chimneys in her stitch. You can smell the wax three streets off. Under the wax: the water.
Bodkin is on the sea-wall like he grew there, sitting where he can see the water, the way he always is. 'You are going to the Wickhouse.' It is not a question.
'Nothing good ever came off that water. Keep your feet dry and your business short — and go in by the wax door, not the water door.' He stays on the stone. 'I don't go in there.'

on_loss_lines: The fog rearranges the streets while I am inside them, and I arrive wet to the elbows and short a card or two.
The Mere got a taste. It will remember me. Ledger that under: mutual.

lines: At the wax door, the fog has residents. One of them is between me and the handle, dry-footed on a wet street.
It is not fast. It does not need to be fast. It is ARRIVING, the way the tide arrives, and the door behind it is the one I need.
The seam is thin out here — I can feel her stitching through the wall, holding. Whatever the Drowned want, it is inside.
In by the wax door. Wax to the rafters — white hills of it, a hundred winters of light not yet sold.
And under the merchant smell, the other one: pond-bottom, old rope, patience. Something lives at the water end of this warehouse, and the wax is not stock. The wax is FEED.
Her seam runs the length of the water wall, stitch after stitch after stitch. Fifteen years I watched her leave at odd hours with her kit. Here is where the hours went.

on_loss_lines: I read her seam the way a kitten reads: out loud, slowly, losing the thread of the thread.
But I keep her count, and the count is the part that matters. The seam and I understand each other now.

steps.title: The Ninth Stray
lines: Her table, years ago. This same chart, half-sewn, and a much smaller cat deployed on top of it as a paperweight.
'Eight I tried, over the years,' she tells the needle, not me. 'Not one of them stayed long enough to finish. The ninth fell asleep on my work, and I took it for a signature.'
She sews around me rather than move me. Count, hook, count, mirror at the turn. I know her hand the way you know weather.
I never once thought to ask what the seam was FOR, or what she meant by the count.
Back in the cold warehouse, her seam in front of me — and it is wrong at the near end. Not torn. Not burned. UNDONE: each stitch lifted out clean, in her own hand, in her own order.
Her order, run BACKWARD. To read what was done here, I have to sew it the way it was unsewn: her stitch, mirrored, back to front.

on_loss_lines: Backward defeats me tonight. It should defeat anybody.
That is the point. I will be thinking about that all the way home.

lines: A hand's length of her thread comes away with the reading — the piece the unpicker lifted and left hanging. Evidence now. Hers, then mine.
The ward did not fail. It was UNPICKED: her exact stitch, mirror-handed, faster than any needle honestly goes. Perfect technique — and Elspeth taught exactly nobody.
Cardew said it: something that learned it from her. Nobody was TAUGHT. So somebody learned without teaching, which is a different crime, with a shorter list of suspects. I do not like how short.
Out by the wax door. Bodkin is gone from the sea-wall; the fog holds his shape for a second, and then does not.
The wax feeds a thing the guild will not name. Her ward holds it. She held the ward, unpaid — and the man who profits from the holding bought her debts.
That is not a coincidence. Coincidence is what mice call carelessness. Wick will see me now; he just does not know it yet.

an_audience_of_wax.name: An Audience of Wax
an_audience_of_wax.board_card: Guildmaster Wick will see you now. Everyone in Wickrow is suddenly very polite. Mind the big one.

lines: A candle arrives at my door. Beeswax, bee seal, wick trimmed to burn exactly one hour: a Chandlers' invitation. You light it and start walking, and if it dies before you arrive, so does the appointment.
The first free Chandlers' light this house has ever seen, offered to the cat. Somebody up the hill has finally done his arithmetic.
I carry it lit through the streets in my teeth, like a comet with dignity problems. Wickrow makes way. Wickrow is suddenly VERY polite.
The Guildhall is a chapel to the bee: ten thousand votives, all lit, the heat of them standing in the room like a body.
Between me and the stairs, the votives' keeper unfolds — a tower of poured wax with a gentle face and hands like warming pans.
'The Guildmaster will see you,' it says, kindly, 'presently.' It takes up the entire floor. Presently is doing a great deal of work in that sentence.
Up the stairs, past the puddle with opinions, into the office: Ellery Wick, small behind a desk built to make everything else smaller, already talking.
'The ward-cat! The seam-mender! Sit — no, not there, the good chair.' He is warm the way his hall is warm: by the burning of something.
'You have questions. Everyone has questions. Ask me anything — you will find I have nothing at all to hide.' Which is what that sentence is always for.
So I put it all on his desk. The stub. The ledger page. The tally. The length of unpicked thread. Item by item, in the order a case is told.

He talks fast, and the books come out, and the books are TRUE, which is the awful part: he bought her debts to buy her BUILDING. The Wickhouse thing is dying; the wax is its last diet; her free wardwork was ruining the price of being afraid of the dark.

'I wanted her EVICTED,' he says, and his voice does its first honest thing all evening: it shakes. 'Evicted, and gone, and alive somewhere cheaper. You do not kill the one needle holding your roof shut. So who ELSE knew the ward was hers?'

Then he shows me the thing he has been sitting on since the night: the counterfoil for his own cart-slot, signed out for Needle Lane — against FAVOR-paper. A debt the Chandlers owed, called in blind. No name asked.
'It came through the usual quiet channels,' he says, quieter himself now. 'Everything in this city comes through the usual quiet channels. One does not ask. The not-asking is what the quiet costs.'
Wick is guilty of everything except the murder. Cross him off. Keep the rest.
He watches me decide what to do with him, which is the most honest fear in the room.
A guild that sells the dark. A warehouse full of teeth. A dead woman's unpaid thread. And a guildmaster who would very much like this conversation to stay between us.
choices: Expose him. The city reads his books at eight bells.
Squeeze him. A guildmaster's knot, tied where the Weft can see.

lines: By eight bells the Lamplighters have his books, and by nine the criers do. Wickrow's little flames gutter with embarrassment. The terror margin dies on the counting-room floor.
Merrow reads the ward-shift page aloud on the hall steps. Twice. The second time slower.
Wick keeps his desk, barely, and hates me with the pure focus of a man who now NEEDS me. Useful, hate like that. It files things.
'Once,' he says, when he sees what I want instead. A knot goes into my thread — a Guildmaster's knot, tied by a man who has never visibly owed anyone anything, hating every loop of it.
Overnight, the Chandlers become exquisitely civil to one particular cat. Civility, from a guild, is an invoice. We will see who ends up paying whom.
The Lamplighters will hear what I did not do with those books. Merrow will say nothing. She will just re-chalk the tally, one stroke shorter.
Home. The board gets its last pin of the season: a counterfoil, and a thread running from it to a gentleman nobody meets.
Favor-paper drains toward Gravamen — where the carts change hands, and the Court keeps ledgers of everything owed. The quiet channels have an address now.
One suspect off the board. One name-that-is-not-a-name waiting on it. The kettle stays quiet, and so, tonight, do I.

night_rounds.name: Night Rounds
night_rounds.board_card: The streets don't watch themselves. Someone ought to be paid for this. Someone is not.

lines: The lamps are short-handed and the dark has noticed. Somebody ought to walk the streets that miss their light.
Nobody pays a cat for this. I do it so the city stays the kind of city I can work. First stop: the gutter on the corner, which is glowing.
Two more down the lane, sharing one appetite between them. Wisps used to be rare on this street.
Used to be.
Last leg, past Number Twelve, where the dog and I keep a standing appointment neither of us has ever missed.

garden_route.name: The Garden Route
garden_route.board_card: Cross the back gardens. Wake nothing. The dahlias are not the danger.

lines: Six gardens between the Shambles and Thimblefield, and the fastest way through all of them is a gate nobody has opened since the old captain died.
It is not locked. It is WOVEN — withies through withies, and whoever did it knew what they were doing.

on_loss_lines: It tightens on me twice and I go over the wall like an amateur, which costs me a claw and all of my composure.
Somebody good made that gate. I would like to meet them and I would like to not.

lines: The gate un-weaves without a whisper. Which leaves the Watch: a goose in the first garden with nothing to do all night but listen.
You cannot unpick a goose. Some things simply have to be argued with.
The gate fought loud, and the first garden heard it: the Watch goose is up, and delighted about it.
Quiet was the plan. The plan has been amended.
Past the goose: the captain's lawn, and the Captain. The chain of office is load-bearing, and the bird underneath it is worse.

empty_coat.name: An Empty Coat
empty_coat.board_card: A coat on Needle Lane is out wearing someone's evening. Object to this.

lines: A coat is out on Needle Lane wearing someone's evening. A Lamplighter's coat, by the cord on the shoulder.
One of the eleven, then. Merrow files their names every week and every week the filings come back marked: no appointment. Not dead. Somewhere.
The wisps have found it first — two of them, drinking the lie of a man who is not there.
The coat has noticed me objecting. It straightens — the way he must have straightened, clocking on.
Whoever wore this is not dead. Missing. The coat remembers the shape of him, and now so do I.
The coat comes quiet in the end. I walk it back to the hall and leave it on its peg, over its boots, toes out, waiting.
Fenn takes it off me at the door — the steadiest round of the four they have left — and hangs it himself, and squares the boots under it, and says nothing.
Nobody says anything. Everybody sees.

the_milk_debt.name: The Milk Debt
the_milk_debt.board_card: A kitten sold her purr to the Quiet Gentleman. The Court of Whiskers considers this Everyone's Problem. Attendance is not optional.

lines: The Court of Whiskers convenes on the ropewalk roof at the wrong hour, on purpose, so that attending is itself a sacrifice.
The docket tonight is small, orange, and asleep on the evidence: Tansy, of the canal litter, who sold her purr to the Quiet Gentleman for the favor that fished her brothers out.
Contract's legal, says the Clowder. Purr's gone. And if the precedent stands, by spring he will hold a MARKET in them.
The kitten wakes up, locates me, and announces to the Court that her counsel has arrived.
I have issued no such appointment. The Court minutes it anyway. Cats have a genius for making your dignity load-bearing.
'He never signs anything that can be settled,' warns the Clowder-mother. 'Read it before you touch it.' Sound advice for contracts, and for him.
The contract lodges where his paper always lodges: a strongroom under the Shambles that smells of sealing-wax and of absolutely nothing else. No guards. His paper guards itself.
There it is. Her purr, in escrow: a knot of thread on a shelf, purring faintly to itself — the saddest sound I have heard in a week of funerals.
And the knot has grown a loop nobody tied. INTEREST. A purr accrues — and a debt owed to itself has its own loose end. Which makes it my kind of paper.

on_loss_lines: The knot tightens twice, and I stop before it swallows the loose end. His work does not break. It COLLECTS.
Not tonight, then. Tonight I sit with the little knot and let it purr at me, and we both pretend that helps.

lines: The purr comes loose like a cork and goes home the way purrs do: all at once, at volume, from somewhere behind the ribs.
Tansy vibrates so hard she falls off the shelf. The Court of Whiskers will call it precedent. She will call it Tuesday.
On the shelf where the knot sat: a calling card. Blank, and smelling faintly of fog. It was not there when I started. Noted, with interest.
I come back the next night, and the next. The loop keeps its slack for me — interest, it turns out, is patient on both sides.
On the third night the knot gives: cork, purr, kitten, volume. Some jobs are won by arithmetic and stubbornness. Most jobs, honestly.
On the shelf where the knot sat: a calling card. Blank, and smelling faintly of fog. It was not there on the first night. Noted, with interest.
Tansy follows me home. I explain that I live alone. She agrees enthusiastically, and moves in.
She has decided she is my apprentice. I have issued no such appointment. She is asleep on my paws as I think this, purring like a small wrong engine, which rather settles the docket.
The Gentleman never signs anything that can be settled. Somewhere tonight a page of his is one line lighter — and I intend to be a great deal more expensive before he and I are done.

the_pigeon_ballot.name: The Pigeon Ballot
the_pigeon_ballot.board_card: The pigeons are holding an election. Somebody is stuffing the ballot. The ballot is a hat. I wish any part of that were a joke.

lines: The Pigeon Post is electing a Postmaster, which happens twice a century and is decided by hat: you perch on the brim of the candidate you back, and the hat that bows lowest wins.
A slick young cock called Toby is winning on cleaner ledges and unlimited seed. The seed is real, and pigeons do not ask where seed comes from.
Here is why it is my problem: the night my witch died, every pigeon in Hollowmere went quiet at once. And quiet, I have lately learned, is a thing that can be BOUGHT.
First, the seed itself: it comes up to the roosts from somewhere, in quantity, carried high and scattered wide.
Follow the trail without being seen following it. Pigeons notice a cat on a roofline the way bankers notice fire.

on_loss_lines: Halfway along a ridgeline the whole flock lifts at once, and I flatten into a chimney's shadow and count the feathers going over.
They know something crossed tonight. They do not know it was me. Half a win. The long way up, then.

lines: The trail ends above Needle Lane: a grain-chute, swept clean, the sweepings arranged a little too neatly to be spillage.

Good seed, bought in bulk, hauled UP. Nobody hauls seed up — seed lives at street level, with the spills and the honest pigeons. This was scattered from above, wide as weather, by somebody with HANDS.
The Perch convenes at moonrise to crown the hat. Time the Post heard what its quiet cost — from the one bird whose pride will not survive lying once the paper is out.

on_loss_lines: The Postmaster out-dignifies me in front of the entire Perch, which I did not know was possible and will be studying.
The count stands. But forty pigeons heard the word 'docket', and pigeons repeat things. Give it a week.

lines: 'We voted with our beaks full, and we called the quiet weather.' From a Postmaster, before the whole Perch, that is not gossip. That is a confession with plumage.
Toby attempts a dignified molt into the crowd and is sat on by his own electors. The hat is impounded pending honesty.
So the murder night had a QUARTERMASTER: somebody fed the city's gossip until it slept, days ahead, with human hands and quiet money. The board's thin gentleman just grew a supply line.
No confession tonight. But I watched the old bird's chest deflate when the docket touched the rail, and a Perch cannot un-see what its Postmaster saw.
The seed came before the night. Scattered wide, from above, by hands. Whoever quieted the pigeons planned my witch's murder the way a clerk plans a shipment.
The Perch will finish this without me. Pride is slower than evidence, but it files the same report in the end.
Elections resume next moon, with fresh hats and a seed audit. Democracy, among pigeons, is self-cleaning if you kick it.
Below, a lamplighter relights Needle Lane, and the first pigeon in a month settles over her old window and says something rude about me. Good. The city is talking again.
Quiet can be bought. Noted, priced, filed. The next time a street goes silent around me, I will know I am standing in somebody's purchase.

the_fish_giver.name: The Fish-Giver Is Late
the_fish_giver.board_card: Pell the Fish-Giver has missed two dawns. Cats don't worry. I am not worried. I am investigating.

lines: Every dawn for eleven years, Pell has set out scraps behind his stall for half the strays in Thimblefield. He calls all of us puss. He has never learned one name and never needed to.
He has now missed two dawns, and the half is assembling on his roof like a jury.
Cats do not worry. I am not worried. I am investigating, which is different, and has better posture.
The stall is shuttered. The man is inside, in the dark, doing day-side arithmetic with his head in his hands.
The trouble is on his door, in paper: rent behind, lease called, seven days. The lease runs through a bank, and the bank — I read the seal twice to be sure — banks for the Chandlers.
Paper again. This city bleeds by paper. Nobody is going to knife the Fish-Giver in his parlor; they are going to FILE him out of it.
He cannot fight paper. Neither can I. But the day-side can be moved by other things, if you know what a street is actually worth.

on_loss_lines: A cat on the roofline at breakfast is conspicuous, and half the street's laundry knows me now.
I get where I am going all the same. Slower. Politer. Watched by sheets.

lines: First asset: the drainpipe behind his stall, and the thing he lost down it nine years ago — his grandmother's brooch, the one he still tells customers about when the fish is slow.
No hand fits that pipe. A paw does. It costs me a wet shoulder, a spider's whole opinion of me, and one bent whisker.
I leave it on his counting-slab where he cannot miss it. Day-side arithmetic changes fast when a dead woman's silver joins in.
Second asset: the pigeons, who owe this street and know where everyone drinks. The landlord's man takes his evenings at the Bent Anchor, and takes them loudly, and has a magistrate for a sister.
Third asset: the magistrate keeps a cat. The cat owes me — a matter of a terrier, never discussed. I sit on her windowsill at dusk and pay the slow blink, and the debt moves.
By morning the magistrate has remembered, for reasons she will never quite place, that eviction schedules have rules, and that her brother's employer has been careless with them.
Dawn, three days later. The shutter goes up. The scraps go down. The jury disperses into a congregation, and Pell stands in the middle of it grinning at nothing, wearing his grandmother on his coat.

'Mind the water, puss,' he says, to all of us, the way he says it every dawn. He never learns my name. He never learns any of it, and that is the point — the day-side must stay the kind of place where luck still happens.
Somebody once put a saucer down for a stray who had nothing to trade for it. The account stays open. It always will.
